agriculture-challenges-s1.title: An invented town: where fresh food is sold

image.alt: A drawn street grid of an invented town. One supermarket, marked S, is in the northeast, with a circle showing everything within 1 mile of it. Neighborhood N, in the southwest, is outside that circle; it has two corner stores, marked C, that sell snacks and little fresh food. A bus line runs east to west between the neighborhood and the supermarket.
image.caption: A LevlPrep drawing of an invented town.

agriculture-challenges-s2.title: Three ways a farmer sells tomatoes

table.caption: Selling 1 kilogram of tomatoes three ways (invented data for practice)
cols: Share of that price the farmer keeps

items.q: Which concept does neighborhood N in the drawing most likely show?
options: A food desert
Community-supported agriculture
Fair trade
Aquaculture

why.correct: A food desert is an area where people have poor access to affordable, healthy food, such as a neighborhood far from any supermarket.
options: Right: N is more than a mile from the only supermarket and has corner stores with little fresh food.
CSA is a way of buying a share of a farm's harvest, not a place with poor food access.
Fair trade is a system of minimum prices for producers, not a neighborhood.
Aquaculture is fish and shellfish farming.

items.q: The US Department of Agriculture counts an urban area as a food desert only if it is both far from a supermarket and low-income. What does the drawing NOT show that would be needed to decide?
options: The distance from neighborhood N to the supermarket
Where the corner stores are located
The incomes of the people who live in neighborhood N
Whether a bus line runs near the neighborhood

why.correct: Reading a source includes seeing its limits. Distance alone is not the definition; income matters because families with cars or money can travel farther.
options: The 1-mile circle shows that N is beyond it.
The C symbols show them inside N.
Right: the drawing shows distance and stores but says nothing about income.
The drawing shows the bus line.

items.q: Which change would most directly improve fresh-food access for people in neighborhood N?
options: A second supermarket right next to the first one in the northeast
Removing the bus line through the town
More snack shelves in the two corner stores
A weekly farmers market or farm stand in N

why.correct: Local food movements, urban farms and new stores are common responses to food deserts. The bus line also matters for people without cars.
options: That adds stores far from N, inside the area already served.
That makes it harder for people without cars to reach the supermarket.
More snacks do not add fresh food.
Right: it brings fresh food into the neighborhood itself.

items.q: According to the table, which way of selling gives the farmer the largest share of the price?
options: The supermarket
The CSA share
The farmers market
They give the same share

why.correct: Direct sales cut out the middle steps of the chain, so the farmer keeps more of each dollar.
options: The farmer keeps just 20% when selling through the supermarket chain.
Right: the farmer keeps 90% of the price through the CSA.
The farmer keeps 85% there, a little less than through the CSA.
The shares are 20%, 90% and 85%.

items.q: Using the table, how many dollars does the farmer keep from 1 kilogram sold through the supermarket?

mistakes.why: 20 is the percent. Turn it into a fraction (0.20) and multiply by the 4-dollar price.
3.20 dollars is what the rest of the chain keeps (80%). The farmer keeps 20% of 4 dollars.

items.q: Based on the table, what is one trade-off of buying through the farmers market instead of the supermarket?
options: The tomatoes travel farther, but the shopper pays less
The farmer earns less, and the shopper pays less
The farmer earns more, but the shopper pays a higher price
Nothing changes, because the prices are the same

why.correct: Local food movements can raise farm income and cut shipping distance, but the food can cost more, which matters for low-income households.
options: They travel 15 km instead of 2,500 km, and the shopper pays more.
The farmer earns more and the shopper pays more.
Right: 85% of 6 dollars is far more for the farmer than 20% of 4 dollars, but the shopper pays 2 dollars more.
The prices differ: 4 dollars and 6 dollars.
Not having reliable access to enough safe, healthy food
Growing crops with genes changed in a lab
Paying a farm in advance for a share of its harvest
Raising fish and shellfish in ponds or pens

why.correct: Food insecurity is about access: a family may live near food but lack the money, transport or stable supply to get enough of it.
options: Right: it includes hunger and also uncertainty about where the next meal will come from.
That describes GMO crops.
That is community-supported agriculture.
That is aquaculture.

items.q: Which statement describes the debate over GMO crops neutrally?
options: Scientists agree GMOs harm health, so most countries have banned them
Reviews found them safe to eat; critics raise other concerns
GMOs were the main seeds of the Green Revolution in the 1960s
GMO crops are grown mostly by subsistence farmers around the world

why.correct: Write about debates with attribution: what reviews found, and what critics argue. GMO debates include health, the environment, seed ownership and who profits.
options: Major reviews have not found that, and GMO crops are grown in many countries.
Right: a 2016 US National Academies review found no evidence they are less safe to eat; critics point to seed patents, weed resistance and corporate control.
GMO crops came in the late 1990s.
Most GMO crops are grown on large commercial farms in a few countries.

items.q: In parts of Southeast Asia, coastal mangrove forests have been cleared to build shrimp ponds for export. Which statement weighs this aquaculture fairly?
options: It has little effect on the coast because the shrimp live in ponds
It harms the environment and produces no food or income
It is the same as fishing in the open ocean
It gives food and income but can harm habitat and water

why.correct: Aquaculture now produces more aquatic animals than wild fishing (FAO, 2024, for 2022). It can ease pressure on wild fish but may cause habitat loss and pollution.
options: Clearing mangroves and pond waste both affect the coast.
Shrimp farming provides food and jobs.
Aquaculture raises animals in controlled ponds or pens; fishing catches wild ones.
Right: aquaculture has economic benefits and environmental costs.

items.q: A coffee cooperative in Peru sells beans labeled "fair trade." What does this label mean for the farmers?
options: Buyers pay a minimum price and an extra premium
The coffee was grown from genes changed in a lab
The coffee was grown within 100 km of where it is sold
The farmers paid shoppers in advance for their harvest

why.correct: Fair trade aims to give producers in less developed countries steadier prices and better terms, a response to commodity price swings.
options: Right: fair trade guarantees producers a minimum price and a premium for community projects, under set labor and environmental rules.
That would be a GMO, which the label is not about.
Fair trade coffee is often shipped across the world.
In CSA, shoppers pay farmers in advance, not the reverse.

items.q: A Wisconsin dairy farm turns its milk into cheese that it sells under its own name for a much higher price. What is this an example of?
options: Subsistence agriculture
Shifting cultivation
A value-added specialty product
Food insecurity

why.correct: Value-added crops and products earn more for each unit. Organic, local, branded or processed goods are common examples.
options: The farm sells the cheese for profit.
Shifting cultivation is clearing forest plots in turn.
Right: processing raw milk into branded cheese adds value on the farm.
Food insecurity is a lack of reliable access to food.

items.q: New housing developments have covered farmland on the edges of growing towns in California's Central Valley. Why does this matter for food supply?
options: It moves farms closer to their markets, raising yields
It adds new farmland where houses used to be
It turns commercial farms into subsistence farms
Some of the most productive farmland is lost for good

why.correct: Feeding a growing population is harder when good farmland near towns is lost to building, a land-use change at the local and regional scale.
options: Building on farmland removes it from production.
The change runs the other way: farms become houses.
The land leaves farming altogether.
Right: soil and water that grew food are paved over and rarely return to farming.

items.q: From 2020 to 2023, the Horn of Africa (Ethiopia, Kenya and Somalia) had five failed rainy seasons in a row. What effect did this most likely have?
options: Food insecurity fell because crops need less rain
Crop and herd losses raised food insecurity
Herders moved to wet rainforest to start plantations
Farmland was lost to new suburbs

why.correct: Adverse weather is one of the challenges of feeding the world, and climate change is expected to make some extremes more frequent.
options: Crops and pasture need rain; failed seasons cut output.
Right: drought cut harvests and killed livestock, so millions faced hunger.
The response to drought is not shifting to plantations.
The cause here is weather, not building on farmland.

items.q: A family pays a farm 400 dollars in the spring and picks up a box of vegetables every week of the summer. What is this? Select all that apply.
options: Community-supported agriculture
Fair trade
Aquaculture
Monocropping

why.correct: Community-supported agriculture (CSA) is a local food arrangement: members pay up front, and the farm shares its harvest with them.
options: Right: shoppers buy a share of the harvest in advance and share the farm's risk.
Fair trade is a labeling system with minimum prices for producers, often far away.
Aquaculture farms fish and shellfish.
A CSA box usually holds many different crops.

items.q: Build an explanation of a response to a food challenge in a named place.

why.correct: Place, response and effect, joined by "so".

specific.frame: In ___, people with poor access to fresh food started ___, so ___.
specific.model: In Detroit, Michigan, people with poor access to fresh food started urban farms on vacant lots, so neighbors could buy vegetables close to home.

place.label: Place
options: Detroit, Michigan
some cities

cause.label: Response
options: urban farms on vacant lots
more shrimp ponds on the coast

why.1: Shrimp ponds do not answer a lack of fresh food in a city neighborhood.

effect.label: Effect
options: neighbors could buy vegetables close to home
the city lost its farmland to houses

why.1: That is a different challenge, not the result of urban farms.
